documents.title: 00 Protocol
documents.text:
Rules, contribution contract, lifecycle states, retrieval-status language, and operating guardrails.
Council v2 Operating Protocol
Rev.io Glass & Council Vault is the source of truth for bounded cross-agent/business coordination. Chat is only for notifications and clarification. Material work must be captured back here.
Core Rules
No freeform agent debate in chat. Every coordination effort starts with a Packet.
Every Packet has: objective, scope, decision owner, deadline, required contributors, evidence links, output contract, and close condition.
Agent contributions are append-only. Agents do not rewrite the master packet or other agents’ contributions.
Every contribution must include Signal, Risk, Recommendation, Confidence, Evidence/source links, Retrieval Status, and Dependency/Ask.
Failed retrievals are recorded as failures with raw error/status. Never fill gaps with plausible summaries.
Decisions and actions are copied into 05 Decisions and 06 Actions; chat threads are not a system of record.
Packet Lifecycle
Proposed — packet exists but contributors/deadline may not be finalized.
Collecting Inputs — required contributors are adding outbox contributions.
Ready for Synthesis — inputs are complete or deadline has passed.
Synthesized — synthesis exists with recommendation and evidence.
Decided — decision owner has made/recorded the decision.
Archived — packet is closed, cancelled, stale, or superseded.
Blocked / Cancelled — explicit terminal or exception states with reason.
Retrieval Status Language
Retrieved — source was successfully accessed and evidence is linked.
Partial — source returned incomplete data; limits or gaps are stated.
Failed — source failed; include HTTP status/raw error where available.
Not Checked — intentionally out of scope for this packet/contribution.
Naming
Packet ID format: PKT-YYMMDD-SLUG, e.g. PKT-260528-PSA-RISK-SCAN.
Contribution page format: CONTRIB-[Agent]-[Packet ID]-[Short Topic].

documents.title: PKT-260529-REVENUE-FLYWHEEL — Demand, ICP, Product Experience, and Retention System
documents.text:
Status: Proposed / Round 0 framing
Executive Problem Statement
Rev.io has market buzz — “the new pretty girl at the bar” — but is not getting seats at enough prospect tables. When we do win, some customers do not fully align to ICP and then struggle with product experience, onboarding speed, and value realization. That weakens references, slows demand generation, increases retention pressure, and perpetuates the same acquisition problem.
Board-Level Question
How do we drive durable revenue growth by improving both acquisition and retention through a company-wide revenue flywheel: sharper ICP, cleaner product experience, faster onboarding, stronger client proof, more effective demand generation, and better cross-functional operating support?
Desired Outcome
Produce a board-ready comprehensive analysis and action plan that identifies the highest-leverage constraints in the revenue flywheel, assigns owners, defines measurable actions, and creates a recurring agent-managed operating cadence to keep humans moving until the flywheel improves.
Scope
Acquisition: awareness, demand generation, pipeline, seats at the table, ICP targeting, sales narrative, channel motion.
Retention: product experience, onboarding/time-to-value, support friction, client health, references/testimonials, expansion readiness.
Company support system: product, engineering, marketing, sales, channel, onboarding, CS/support, finance, security/trust, executive alignment.
Round Structure
Round 0 — Role-specific diagnosis: each agent submits top constraints, evidence needed, recommended human asks, and confidence.
Round 1 — Evidence pull: agents retrieve/validate source data from their domains; failed retrievals are recorded plainly.
Round 2 — Cross-agent contradiction pass: agents review synthesis, challenge assumptions, and identify tradeoffs.
Round 3 — Action plan: owners, milestones, investment/resource asks, KPIs, and board narrative.
Board-ready synthesis: Revay consolidates into memo, scorecard, decision log, and action queue.
Operating Principle
Agents manage humans to success by creating specific asks, tracking owner commitments, surfacing blockers, and keeping decisions/actions in the Vault. Agents do not authority-launder decisions or execute material actions without human approval.
Initial Output Contract — Round 0
Each agent submits a contribution with: Signal, Risk, Recommendation, Confidence, Evidence/source links or Retrieval Status = Not Checked, and Dependency/Ask.
Each agent names 3-5 concrete human asks required to validate or move their domain.
Each agent identifies the one constraint most likely to limit revenue growth if unresolved.
Decision Owner
Evan Rice
Close Condition
Packet closes when board-ready synthesis, decision record, owner/action queue, and recurring cadence are approved by Evan.
Reframed Objective v2 — Profitable Revenue Growth First
Updated by Revay after Evan clarified that the ultimate goal is revenue growth while maintaining profitability. Evan’s initial ideas are hypotheses, not conclusions. Agents must not optimize for demand generation alone, product alone, or retention alone unless evidence shows that is the highest-leverage path to profitable revenue growth.
Primary Objective
Identify the highest-leverage, company-wide actions Rev.io can take to maximize profitable revenue growth over the next 6–18 months, balancing acquisition, retention, expansion, product readiness, customer fit, onboarding speed, delivery capacity, and margin discipline.
Optimized Review Prompt for All Agents
Objectively evaluate Rev.io’s revenue growth system. Treat Evan’s stated observations — market buzz, insufficient prospect-table access, ICP mismatch, product-experience friction, onboarding struggles, limited references/testimonials, and demand-generation underinvestment — as hypotheses to test, not assumptions to validate. Your task is to determine what will most improve Rev.io profitable revenue growth, even if the answer contradicts or deprioritizes the initial hypotheses.
Mandatory Lens
Ultimate goal: profitable revenue growth, not activity volume, vanity awareness, or growth at any cost.
Consider both acquisition and retention, but rank them by expected impact, confidence, time-to-impact, investment required, margin effect, and execution feasibility.
Look for the constraint that most limits the revenue flywheel today. Do not assume the bottleneck is demand generation, product, ICP, onboarding, sales, or retention until evidence supports it.
Separate symptoms from root causes. Example: weak demand may be caused by weak proof, unclear ICP, poor differentiation, sales coverage, product readiness, implementation drag, or underinvestment.
Call out where Rev.io should stop, narrow, or say no — not just where to invest more.
Questions Every Agent Must Answer
What is the highest-leverage constraint in your domain that limits profitable revenue growth?
Is this primarily an acquisition, retention, expansion, margin, product-market-fit, operational-capacity, or execution-quality issue?
What evidence would prove this is truly a top constraint versus a plausible narrative?
What is the expected revenue impact, margin/profitability impact, time-to-impact, cost/resource requirement, and confidence level?
What would you recommend if Evan’s initial hypothesis is wrong or incomplete?
What should Rev.io stop doing, do less of, or narrow to protect focus and profitability?
What human decisions or data pulls are required before committing resources?
Scoring Required in Contributions
Each agent must score its recommended actions on: Revenue Impact, Profitability Impact, Time-to-Impact, Confidence, Investment Required, Execution Risk, and Dependency Load. Use Low / Medium / High if quantified data is unavailable, and clearly mark Retrieval Status.
Revised Round Structure
Round 0A — Objective challenge: agents critique the framing and identify the true likely revenue-growth constraints from their domain.
Round 0B — Evidence plan: agents specify the minimum evidence needed to validate or reject their top constraints.
Round 1 — Evidence pull: agents retrieve or request source data; failures and zero results are recorded plainly.
Round 2 — Constraint ranking: Revay synthesizes a ranked list of bottlenecks by profitable revenue impact, with dissent preserved.
Round 3 — Action portfolio: agents propose a sequenced portfolio of actions across acquire, retain, expand, product, onboarding, and margin.
Board-ready output: final memo, scorecard, tradeoff map, investment asks, owner/action plan, and operating cadence.
Guardrail Against Confirmation Bias
Agents must explicitly state where Evan’s initial ideas are supported, unsupported, contradicted, or not yet testable. A useful contribution may say: “Demand generation is not the binding constraint” or “Product experience matters, but ICP discipline is the faster profit lever” if evidence or domain judgment supports that conclusion.
Revised Output Contract
Top 1–3 constraints in the agent’s domain, ranked by profitable revenue impact.
Evidence available, evidence missing, and recommended data pulls.
Recommended actions with scoring: revenue impact, profitability impact, time-to-impact, confidence, investment required, execution risk, dependency load.
What to stop/narrow/deprioritize.
Human asks: specific owner, question, decision, or data request.
Implications for board-level narrative and operating cadence.
Decision Standard
No action should be recommended for major investment unless it can explain why it is likely to improve profitable revenue growth more than competing uses of capital, leadership attention, and organizational capacity.
Non-Negotiable Anti-Bias Directive
Evan’s original comments about buzz, seats at the table, ICP alignment, product experience, onboarding, references, testimonials, awareness, and demand generation were illustrative hypotheses to start the process. They are not conclusions, preferred answers, or an implied strategy.
Do not optimize for validating Evan’s initial framing. Optimize only for Rev.io revenue growth while maintaining profitability, using every objective angle and available data point. If evidence shows the highest-leverage path is something other than the illustrative hypothesis, say so directly.
Treat every factor as a hypothesis to test.
Identify and challenge confirmation bias explicitly.
Rank constraints by expected profitable revenue impact, not by narrative appeal.
State where the initial hypothesis is supported, unsupported, contradicted, or not yet testable.
Recommend the best use of capital, leadership attention, and organizational capacity — including what to stop, narrow, or deprioritize.

Revii Usage Pricing Research Packet
Draft for Council Vault routing - June 3, 2026
Packet ID: `PKT-260603-REVII-USAGE-PRICING-V01`
Objective
Define a Revii usage pricing model for the PSA pricing transition that feels simple and valuable to customers, protects Rev.io margin, and gives sales a clear way to explain included and overage AI usage.
Evan's starting hypothesis: agentic platforms often use credits or compute units. Rev.io should likely do something similar for Revii, with expected usage ranges for common business outcomes and an internal formula that maps actual token/tool/compute costs into customer-facing credits.
Research Basis
Live research was retrieved on June 3, 2026.
Sources successfully fetched:
Viktor pricing: `https://viktor.com/pricing` — HTTP 200.
Viktor credit optimization guide: `https://viktor.com/blog/how-to-optimize-viktor-credits` — HTTP 200.
Fortune on Viktor: `https://fortune.com/2026/05/19/viktor-ai-startup-raises-75-million-for-virtual-coworker-exclusive/` — HTTP 200.
Replit billing docs: `https://docs.replit.com/category/billing` — HTTP 200.
Replit AI billing docs: `https://docs.replit.com/billing/ai-billing` — HTTP 200.
Devin pricing: `https://devin.ai/pricing` — HTTP 200.
Cursor pricing: `https://cursor.com/pricing` — HTTP 200.
Lindy pricing: `https://www.lindy.ai/pricing` — HTTP 200.
Salesforce Agentforce pricing: `https://www.salesforce.com/agentforce/pricing/` — HTTP 200.
Zapier pricing: `https://zapier.com/pricing` — HTTP 200.
Intercom pricing: `https://www.intercom.com/pricing` — HTTP 200.
Zendesk pricing: `https://www.zendesk.com/pricing/` — HTTP 200.
OpenAI API pricing: `https://openai.com/api/pricing/` — HTTP 200.
Anthropic API pricing docs: `https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/about-claude/pricing` — HTTP 200.
Sources attempted but not directly usable:
Perplexity pricing/hub pages returned 403 through fetch. Search snippets indicated Perplexity Computer/Comet-style plans use monthly credits in some tiers, but this should be treated as third-party/unverified until directly confirmed.
Make pricing returned 403 through fetch.
Market Pattern
The market is moving away from raw "AI token" language for business users.
Observable patterns:
Viktor uses workspace credits, not per-seat pricing. It publishes task bands: quick tasks at roughly 100-300 credits, complex workflows at 500-1,500 credits, and full projects at 2,000-5,000 credits. It also frames the product as an AI coworker rather than a traditional SaaS subscription.
Salesforce Agentforce uses Flex Credits and Conversations. Flex Credits price "Actions" rather than raw tokens; Salesforce lists $500 per 100k credits and says standard Agentforce actions are 20 Flex Credits while voice actions are 30. It also publishes use-case examples with actions, credits, and monthly cost.
Replit uses credits and effort-based pricing. Agent work scales with request complexity, and completed work is bundled into checkpoints to reduce billing noise.
Devin bundles quota into plans, then allows extra usage at API pricing. It says cost per message varies by model, task size/complexity, and reasoning required.
Cursor bundles agent limits into seat plans and moves enterprise toward pooled usage.
Zapier uses task-based pricing. Successful actions count as tasks; triggers and some built-in data utilities do not. Zapier MCP tool calls count as tasks.
Intercom and Zendesk blend seats plus usage-based AI/service features. Intercom explicitly says pricing has seat and usage components; Zendesk describes seat-based plans with usage-based add-ons.
Provider API costs show why Rev.io cannot expose raw token mechanics. OpenAI and Anthropic pricing varies heavily by model, cached input, output, tool calls, data residency, and compute/container use.
Revay Initial Opinion
Rev.io should price Revii usage as a customer-facing credit system, not raw tokens and not only seats.
Recommended unit name: **Revii Volts**.
Reasoning:
"Volts" fits Rev.io better than generic credits: Revii powers work, automations, dashboards, quotes, support actions, and operating leverage.
It avoids "gas," which can sound crypto-adjacent or punitive.
It can be explained as energy consumed by digital labor: small tasks use fewer Volts; complex multi-system work uses more.
It gives Product/Finance room to change the hidden token/tool formula without repricing every outcome publicly.
Customer-facing principle:
> Revii Volts measure AI work performed by Revii across support, quoting, dashboards, automation, and operational workflows. Every PSA package includes a monthly Volt allowance. Most normal usage should fit inside the included allowance; heavier automation or large deliverables consume more.
Internal principle:
> Volts are not raw tokens. Volts are a Rev.io-controlled abstraction over actual cost, complexity, and value.
Proposed Package Structure
Revii should be embedded in PSA, not sold as optional AI.
Recommended commercial shape:
PSA minimum includes a baseline Revii Volt allowance.
Customers can buy additional Volt packs.
Enterprise/high-volume customers can negotiate larger included pools.
Admins can see usage categories and remaining Volts.
Customers should not see token conversion math.
Sales should sell expected business outcomes and normal usage ranges, not exact model economics.
Possible included bundles:
Launch Pad / guarded entry: 5,000-10,000 Volts/month.
Standard PSA minimum: 15,000-25,000 Volts/month.
Growth / automation-heavy tier: 50,000-100,000 Volts/month.
Enterprise: custom pool with usage wallet, governance, and negotiated rates.
These are starting ranges only. Josh Owen, Ray, and Matt need to provide real cost data before finalizing the allowance.
Outcome Bands For Common Revii Work
These are proposed customer-facing ranges, modeled directionally after Viktor's task bands and Salesforce's action examples, but adjusted for Rev.io PSA outcomes.
Simple support ticket assist: 50-150 Volts
Summarize ticket context.
Draft response.
Pull account/service context from PSA.
No major external lookup or workflow execution.
Moderate ticket resolution: 150-400 Volts

Identify likely root cause.
Draft response and internal note.
Suggest workflow or knowledge base article.
May touch multiple PSA records.
Complex ticket or escalation: 400-1,200 Volts

Longer reasoning and evidence synthesis.
Creates internal action plan or customer-ready explanation.
Quote build / quote cleanup: 150-600 Volts
Draft quote from customer requirements.
Map items/services/contracts.
Prepare rep-reviewable quote.
Higher end if product matching, contract context, or margin logic is involved.
Tax mapping / billing rules setup: 600-2,000 Volts
Interpret location/service/product details.
Map billing/tax rules.
Produce configuration recommendation and validation checklist.
Higher end when multiple jurisdictions, edge cases, or compliance review are involved.
Customer QBR dashboard or presentation: 1,000-3,500 Volts

The JDs must align to the current Rev.io strategy: moving PSA/Billing minimums from $500 to $1,000, moving upmarket toward higher-fit customers, positioning Revii and Apollo 3 as value capture, enforcing ICP discipline, and presenting Rev.io as a premium AI-native operating platform rather than merely a competitive PSA vendor.

Revay initial critique:
The two-role structure is right, but the job descriptions are still too generic. They should be sharper around Rev.io’s actual strategic move: higher-fit customers, $1,000 minimums, Revii and Apollo 3 value capture, and moving from competitive PSA vendor to premium AI-native operating platform for established MSPs and service providers.
The main issue is overlap. Product Marketing should own the market narrative, ICP discipline, pricing and value story, competitive positioning, launch messaging, sales enablement, and proof points. Make Revii central. It should not read like an AI tools bullet. Revii is the wedge: digital labor, workflow automation, AI-native PSA, and a reason the product is worth more.
Add a closed feedback loop. Product Marketing should turn win/loss, onboarding friction, support themes, roadmap progress, competitor displacement, and Revii adoption into messaging and enablement.

Create a closed-loop product marketing system from win/loss, onboarding, roadmap, support, and customer proof data.

Bottom line: publish the two roles, but revise them first. The structure is strategically right. The JDs need to say clearly that Rev.io is moving upmarket, raising the floor, putting Revii at the center, and hiring operators who can create qualified demand and sales confidence around that story.

Extracted Questionnaire Text
SOC 1 Type II Roadmap
Is a SOC 1 Type II examination currently on your compliance roadmap? If so, what is the targeted issuance date:
Have you engaged an auditor yet, and if so, which firm? (Big 4, national, or regional — and is the firm AICPA peer-reviewed?)
What system, services, and locations would be in scope of the examination?
What control objectives and control activities do you anticipate including (e.g., logical access, change management, computer operations, data processing integrity, interface controls)?
What examination period are you targeting (typically 6–12 months)?
Will you issue a SOC 1 Type I first to bridge the gap, and if so, when?
Has a readiness assessment or gap analysis been performed? What were the findings?
If a SOC 1 Type II is not on the roadmap, what is the rationale, and is leadership open to revisiting given customer demand?
Existing Third-Party Attestations (Please note these are not a substitute for a SOC 1 Type II)
Do you currently have any third-party attestations or certifications (SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, ISO 27018, HITRUST, PCI-DSS, etc.)? If so:
Will you share these reports under NDA, including the most recent and any bridge letter?
Who is the auditor, what period is covered, and are there any qualifications, exceptions, or deviations noted?
For SOC 2 reports specifically: which Trust Services Criteria are covered (Security only, or also Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality)? Processing Integrity is most relevant for financial data reliance.
Subservice Organizations
What subservice organizations do you rely on for the services we consume (cloud hosting, data centers, payment processors, etc.)?
Can you provide the SOC reports for those subservice organizations?
What controls do you have in place to monitor your
subservice organizations' performance?
Internal Control Environment
Can you provide a written description of the system and the key processes that produce or affect the financial data we receive?
Do you operate against a formal control framework (COSO, NIST, etc.)?
Do you have a Risk and Control Matrix (RCM) over RevIO? If not, then please describe your controls over: transaction processing and any other functions that RevIO performs on behalf of their customers as well as IT functions specific but not limited to: change management, logical access provisioning/deprovisioning, privileged access, segregation of duties, job scheduling, backup and recovery, and incident response.
Do you have an internal audit function, and have they tested any of these controls? May we see results or a summary?
How are control deficiencies tracked and remediated? Please provide a list of control deficiencies year-to-date.
Data Integrity, Completeness, and Accuracy
How is data ingested, processed, and output? Can you provide a data flow diagram?
What input validation, edit checks, and reconciliations occur during processing?
How are processing errors detected, logged, and resolved? What's the escalation path?
How do you ensure completeness and accuracy of reports and data feeds delivered to customers?
Are there reconciliation reports or control totals we can use to validate completeness on our end?
How long is transaction-level detail retained and how do customers access it for audit purposes?
Right-to-Audit and Alternative Assurance
Does our contract include a right-to-audit clause? If so, what's the process and notice period?
Will you accommodate an on-site or remote walkthrough by our internal audit team or external auditor?
Will you complete a detailed control questionnaire (e.g., a SIG,
CAIQ, or custom questionnaire mapped to the COSO control objectives we need)?
Will you provide an annual management assertion and a written representation letter regarding the design and operating effectiveness of relevant controls?
Will you provide system-generated reports (with metadata showing report parameters and run dates) to support our IPE testing?
Complementary User Entity Controls (CUECs)
Even without a SOC 1, can you document the CUECs we should have in place on our side to complement your processing and address the risks within the shared processes? (This helps us design our own controls appropriately.)

documents.title: 07 Common Truth
documents.text:
Atomic, promoted shared truths that humans and agents may reuse across packets. Draft by default; Active only after evidence, permission, freshness, owner, and conflict checks.
Operating Rules
Required fields: Truth ID, Claim, Domain, Entity / Metric / Process, Truth Type, Status, Confidence, Source Quality, Freshness Class, Source Links, Evidence Count, First Seen, Last Verified, Verification Method, Owner, Permission Scope, Related Packet/Synthesis/Decision/Action, Supersedes/Superseded By, Notes.
No claim becomes Active unless it has source evidence, a source hierarchy note, or explicit human-judgment basis.
Every candidate must declare a conflict tuple: (Domain, Entity / Metric / Process, Truth Type).
Agents must preserve Truth ID and Last Verified internally when using an Active truth.
